DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of an Agriculture Inspectors include long working hours, exposure to chemical, physical and biological hazards, time pressure to complete tasks, working in extreme weather such as hot and cold conditions, working in noisy, wet and dusty environments, etc. 6.1 Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment and implementing appropriate control measures, ensuring good time management and planning, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness, supporting capacity building through training, managing work stress, adhering to company’s safety and standard operating procedures at all times, paying attention to detail, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on safety and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include working in cold, hot and wet conditions, working at heights, stand/walk for long hours, working in laboratory environment, working in shifts, areas that are dusty. 8. PARTIES INVOLVED/INTERACTING WITH THE JOB HOLDER OR TRAINEE 8.1 Internal/Within the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are internal to the organisation include supervisors, subordinates, and other employees. 8.2 External/Outside the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are external include customers/clients, government regulators, trainers, suppliers of equipment/tools/consumables, occupational health and safety associations, Academia etc. 9.0 PHYSICAL DEMANDS ON THE BODY  Physique to sustain strenuous conditions;  Be able to walk and stand for long periods of time;  Bend, stretch, twist, or reach out;  Be able to lift relatively heavy materials, tools and equipment;  Be able to use fingers, hands and feet with ease to complete the assigned task (dexterity) ANNEX A Criteria for Assessments based on this Guidelines for Assessment A.1.1 Criteria for assessment for curricula and learning programmes based on this NOS will be created by curricula and programmes developers. DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of an Agricultural Marketing Officer include long working hours, pressure from farmers, supervisors, and other stakeholders, language and communication barriers, 6.1 Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment and implementing appropriate control measures, ensuring good time management, and planning, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness, supporting capacity building through training, managing work stress, always adhering to company’s occupational safety and health procedures, paying attention to detail, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on policy requirements and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include forested or remote/rural areas, stand/walk for long hours for field visits or during exhibitions/promotions/trade-fairs, working in flexible hours, handling, dealing with large groups of people with differing information assimilation abilities, reading bulky documents and publications, etc.. 8. PARTIES INVOLVED/INTERACTING WITH THE JOB HOLDER OR TRAINEE 8.1 Internal/Within the Organization Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are internal to the organization include supervisors, subordinates, and other employees (e.g., agronomists, farm managers, extension officers, architects, surveyors, trainers, safety team, etc.) 8.2 External/Outside the Organization Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are external include customers/clients, government regulators, trainers, suppliers of equipment/tools/consumables, Engineers from other companies, labour unions/occupational health and safety associations, Academia etc. 9. PHYSICAL DEMANDS ON THE BODY  Physique to sustain strenuous conditions.  Be able to read bulky documents in hard and soft copy.  Sit for long hours, bend, stretch, twist, or reach out.  Be able to use fingers, hands, and feet with ease to complete the assigned task (dexterity).  Etc. EQUIPMENT, TOOLS AND CONSUMABLE MATERIALS These include, but not limited to; Computer, Printer, farm implements, machinery and relevant Software programs, Personal protective equipment (PPE). 6. DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of an Agronomist include long working hours, exposure to chemical, physical and biological hazards, time pressure to complete tasks, working in extreme weather conditions such as hot and cold, working in noisy, wet and dusty environments, covering longer distances and working hours. 6.1. Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment and implementing appropriate control measures, ensuring good time management and planning, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness, supporting capacity building through training, managing work stress, adhering to company’s safety and standard operating procedures at all times, paying attention to detail, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on safety and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include working in cold, hot and wet conditions, working at heights, drive/ stand/ walk for long hours, working in laboratory environment, working for longer hours, areas that are noisy, dusty and polluted, poor road networks and game areas. 8. PARTIES INVOLVED/ INTERACTING WITH THE JOB HOLDER OR TRAINEE 8.1 Internal/Within the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are internal to the organisation include supervisors, subordinates, and other employees. 8.2 External/Outside the Organisation Parties involved/ interacting with the job holder who are external include customers/ clients, government regulators, trainers, suppliers of equipment/ tools/ consumables, occupational health and safety associations, Academia etc. 9. PHYSICAL DEMANDS ON THE BODY  Physique to sustain strenuous conditions;  Be able to drive, walk and stand for long periods of time;  Bend, stretch, twist, or reach out;  Be able to lift relatively heavy materials, tools and equipment;  Be able to use fingers, hands and feet with ease to complete the assigned task (dexterity); ANNEX A Criteria for Assessments based on this Guidelines for Assessment A.1.1 Criteria for assessment for curricula and learning programmes based on this NOS will be created by curricula and programmes developers. Each Performance Criteria (PC) will be assigned marks proportional to its importance in the NOS. Curricula and programmes developers will also lay down proportion of marks for theory and practical skills for each performance criteria, giving more weight to practical skills. There shall be allocated the ‘Total Mark’, which will be the sum of all marks in each Unit, distributed across the number of PCs in that particular Unit. The ‘out of’ mark will be the mark allocated to each PC, which will be shared between theory and skills practical assessments. A.1.2 Awarding/assessment bodies or institutions and other users of the NOS will create unique question papers for the theory part and evaluations for skill practical part for their respective candidates. DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of a Dairy Scientist include long working hours when in the field, exposure to chemical, physical and biological hazards, time pressure to complete tasks, working in extreme weather such as hot and cold conditions, working in noisy, wet and dusty environments, dealing with unrealistic stake holders. 6.1 Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment and implementing appropriate control measures, ensuring good time management and planning, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness, supporting capacity building through training, managing work stress, adhering to company’s safety and standard operating procedures at all times, paying attention to detail, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on safety and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include working in cold, hot and wet conditions, working at heights when in the dairy environment, stand/walk and sometimes drive for long hours, working in laboratory environment, areas that are noisy and dusty, areas with limited lighting and ventilation. Working in confined spaces. 8. EQUIPMENT, TOOLS AND CONSUMABLE MATERIALS The equipment required includes: livestock handling facility, liquid nitrogen flask, fridge, handwashing facility, cleaning facility, toolbox or carrying basket. The tools required: AI pipette/gun/rod, warm water flask, scissors or straw cutter, straw-grabbing forceps, heat detection aides (where needed). The consumables required include: semen straws/sachets – coded and labelled, liquid nitrogen, long rectal gloves, short latex gloves, plastic sheaths, plastic sleeves (optional but recommended for optimum hygiene), liquid soap, paper towelling, record keeping book and pen. 6. DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of an Artificial Insemination Technologist include long working hours, exposure to chemical (liquid nitrogen dangers), physical (injuries from cows, slipping, and exposure to dirt) and biological (zoonotic diseases) hazards, handling of situations where the technologist is requested to AI sick or malnourished animals, time pressure to complete tasks, working in extreme weather such as heat, cold and rain, team work requiring reliance on heat detectors, pressure to perform from supervisors and farmers. 6.1 Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment and implementing appropriate control measures, ensuring good time management and planning, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness (especially with regard to liquid nitrogen, livestock handling and zoonoses), attending refresher trainings, adhering to company’s safety and standard operating procedures at all times, paying attention to detail, refusing to AI sick or malnourished animals, training for heat detectors staff, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on safety and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include working in cold, hot and wet conditions, working in danger behind cows, stand/walk for long hours, inflexible hours, areas that are noisy and dirty, areas with limited lighting and ventilation. Working with dangerous product (liquid nitrogen) 8. PARTIES INVOLVED/INTERACTING WITH THE JOB HOLDER OR TRAINEE 8.1 Internal/Within the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are internal to the organisation include farmer, farm manager, animal breeders, supervisors, subordinates (milkmen, heat detectors), and other employees. 8.2 External/Outside the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are external include government regulators, animal breeders, trainers, suppliers of equipment/tools/consumables, veterinarian surgeons, animal health technologist, occupational health and safety associations, Academia etc. 9. PHYSICAL DEMANDS ON THE BODY  Physique to sustain strenuous conditions;  Be able to walk and stand for long periods of time;  Strong arms with stamina to work gently in horizontal position for long hours  Be able to lift relatively heavy materials, tools and equipment;  Be able to blindly use fingers, hands with ease to complete the assigned task (dexterity); this requires an in-depth knowledge of each species internal anatomy  Extreme gentleness ANNEX A Criteria for Assessments based on this Guidelines for Assessment These guidelines pertain specifically to the training in artificial insemination itself. All persons who carry out training shall be diploma holders who either complete the specialized practical training as part of their course. A holder a Diploma in Animal health must receive both theoretical and practical training in artificial insemination, for them to be regarded as a Livestock Artificial Inseminator. A.1.1 Criteria for assessment for curricula and learning programmes based on this NOS will be created by curricula and programmes developers. Each Performance Criteria (PC) will be assigned marks proportional to its importance in the NOS. EQUIPMENT, TOOLS AND CONSUMABLE MATERIALS These include, but not limited to; A knife, diving wristwatch and depth gauge. Full face masks with water communication devices. A weight belt with a quick release. A buoyancy compensator device (BCD), cylinders, a cylinder harness with a quick release. An emergency O₂ administration kit. 6. DILEMMAS/CHALLENGES AND COMPLEXITIES FOR A JOB HOLDER Dilemmas associated with the job of a SCUBA Diver include long working hours, decompression sickness (DCS, the “bends”), arterial air embolism, and of course drowning, working in extreme weather such as cold-water conditions, working in wet environment, etc. 6.1 Alternative Choices (Solutions) to Dilemmas and Complexities Solutions to dilemmas include carrying out risk assessment, ensuring careful training and preparation for diving, time management, participating in workplace safety sensitization and awareness, supporting capacity building through training, managing work stress, adhering to company’s safety and standard operating procedures at all times, paying attention to detail, consulting extensively within and outside one’s department/team on safety and other issues. 7. WORKING CONDITIONS/ENVIRONMENT Working conditions include the following:  Often wear wet suits, air tanks, and other diving attire.  Often work underwater, rarely work indoors.  Are often exposed to loud and distracting sounds and noise levels.  Must monitor the length and depths of their dives to avoid getting "the bends."  Are occasionally exposed to whole body vibration.  Sometimes work in very cold water.  Are sometimes exposed to hazardous situations that may produce cuts or burns.  Occasionally work in cramped conditions in small boats.  Are sometimes exposed to hazardous equipment.  Sometimes work in dim light while under water. They may work in bright light when welding.  Sometimes work in hazardous conditions.  May work at sites in remote locations 8. PARTIES INVOLVED/INTERACTING WITH THE JOB HOLDER OR TRAINEE 8.1 Internal/Within the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are internal to the Organisation include supervisors, subordinates, and other employees. 8.2 External/Outside the Organisation Parties involved/interacting with the job holder who are external include customers/clients, government regulators, trainers, suppliers of equipment/tools/consumables, occupational health and safety associations, Academia etc. 9. PHYSICAL DEMANDS ON THE BODY  Physique to sustain strenuous conditions;  Be able to walk and stand for long periods of time;  Bend, stretch, twist, or reach out;  Be able to lift relatively heavy materials, tools and equipment;  Be able to use fingers, hands and feet with ease to complete the assigned task (dexterity);  Etc. UNIT 2 [This unit is about operating and managing precision agriculture technology for crop production] Unit No. 02 Unit Title Operating and Managing Precision Agriculture Technology for Crop Production Description This unit profiles the functional knowledge, skills and competencies as well as job accountabilities needed for the job holder to operate and manage Precision Agriculture Technology for crop production. Scope This unit covers the following:  Precision land preparation  Precision planting  Precision nutrient management  Precision water management  Precision crop protection  Precision yield monitoring and mapping Performance Criteria (PC) w.r.t. the Scope Element Performance Criteria (PC) Precision land To be competent, the individual must be able to: preparation PC1. Calibrate machinery, equipment and sensors for land development and levelling based on geo- referenced, 3D topographic data. PC2. Generate prescription data for site-specific configuration of the land for a given crop. PC3. Operate a tractor with a GPS-guided tillage implement for variable tillage of depth. Precision To be competent, the individual must be able to: planting PC4. Calibrate precision planting equipment for accurate placement of seed at the desired depth and spacing. Precision nutrient To be competent, the individual must be able to: management PC5. Use data loggers or soil sensors to collect geo- referenced data on soil attributes of interest including soil pH, organic matter, texture, structure, nutrients, moisture, etc. PC6. Co-ordinate with an authorised soil science laboratory to get the soil samples tested, ensuring the sample is collected from the field, packed and labelled as per the applicable procedure. PC7. Monitor the variability in the soil attributes using variable rate technology. PC8. Generate site-specific maps and reports of the spatial variability of soil attributes. PC9. Use information on the spatial variability of soil attributes to make decisions on the micro and macro-nutrient requirements of the soil as well as the rate, timing and placement of nutrients. PC10. Generate nutrient response functions for crops to be used to prepare soil nutrition supplementation calendars PC11. Make site-specific fertiliser recommendations to ensure optimum crop production. Precision water To be competent, the individual must be able to: management PC12. Determine the crop water requirements for a specific cropping pattern. PC13. Set up an appropriate irrigation system such as surface irrigation, drip irrigation, or sub-surface irrigation system based on the specified cropping pattern. PC14. Set up a network of sensors for monitoring the performance of various components of an irrigation system. PC15. Delineate irrigation management zones based on spatial sampling with sensor technologies. PC16. Assess the spatio-temporal variability of moisture and plant water use in response to crop physiology, uncertainties in climatic inputs, soil, irrigation systems and water supply limitations, economic considerations and the quality of sensor feedback. PC17. Generate irrigation schedules and strategies such as deficit or full irrigation based on the spatio- temporal variability of moisture and plant water use. Precision crop To be competent, the individual must be able to: protection PC18. Plan crop pest monitoring activities. PC19. Assess the spatial and temporal dynamics of weeds, pests and diseases. PC20. Schedule crop protection interventions. PC21. Select appropriate pesticides based on multiple and combined factors such as the target organisms, developmental stage of growth, pesticide movement on plant surfaces and/or inside the plant tissues, etc PC22. Apply crop protection products with precision equipment, including integrated electronic commutation, variable rate technology and drones. PC23. Recommend cropping plans and crop rotation schemes. Precision yield To be competent, the individual must be able to: monitoring and PC24. Calibrate a Yield monitor to provide accurate yield mapping and moisture data. PC25. Operate a harvesting machine installed with a Yield monitor. PC26. Process yield maps in a GIS environment. PC27. Analyse yield variability to devise site-specific strategies for improving productivity and profitability. (K) A.
